label: text
text: "I put it to you that the Bank you say you were about to start is a myth and that it is a cloak under which you intended to cover this conspiracy to defraud the Wing. On Bank," said Mr. F. C. Jenkin this morning in the course of searching examination of the first defendant in the Wing On Bank case, as to the operation of the account which he said he opened with the Industrial and Commercial Bank for the purpose of starting a Bank.

label: text
text: Before commencing his cross-examination of the witness, Mr. Jenkin made reference to a paragraph which had appeared in this morning's newspapers in one instance under the headline "Tam Lay Bolts," stating that he, Mr. Jenkin, had said at the afternoon's hearing that the witness, Tam Lay had, in fact, bolted. No statement to that effect was made. What he had stated was that there had not been time to get the witness for appearance at the opening at 2-15 but that he had been seen by solicitors on the other side and other witnesses of the Naval Yard, who had satisfied themselves as to his bona fides.

label: text
text: His Lordship: The Press must be more careful on I may have to take notice. Such mistakes should not be allowed to occur. Mr. Jenkin then continued his cross-examination of the first defendant.

label: text
text: Witness was handed exhibit "Emma" and "Nina."

label: text
text: Mr. Jenkin: Do you or do you not say that the lapel on the cover of "Himina" was ever to your knowledge on the cover of "Nina."

label: text
text: Witness: That I do not know Mr. Jenkin: I put it to you that that label on "Emma" was on the cover of exhibit "Nina" when it was issued to you.

label: text
text: Witness: That also I do not know.

label: text
text: Mr. Jenkin: I put it to you that after you got the book "Nina," you or somebody on your behalf removed the label and put it on the book "Emma."

label: text
text: Mr. Jenkins: I put it to you that you or somebody connected with you then put the label on to "Emma."

label: text
text:
Witness: I did not do it, nor anybody on my behalf.
Mr. Jenkin: I put it to you that you knew when the label was put on to "Emma" that "Emma" was a forgery.

label: text
text: Mr. Jenkin: I put it to witness that on May 3, 1923, he or somebody on his behalf entered in the book "Emma" an account with the "Wing On Bank"

label: text
text:
Counsel's Objection Uphold.
Mr. Zeitlyn objected to this question and His Lordship upheld the objection. It involved an implication that he was aware of something he had denied.

label: text
text: Mr. Jenkin: I put it to you that you or someone on your behalf then got $27,000 from that book.

label: text
text: Mr. Jenkin: I put it to you that you or someone on your behalf presented the book the next day and got $23,000.

label: text
text: Witness: I did not, neither did I ask anybody else to.

label: paragraph_title
text: BUNGALOW THEFT.

label: text
text: Money and jewellery amounting to $5,820 have been stolen from the residence of Mr. M. Takeuchi, No. 18, Macdonnell Road. Mr. Takeuchi, who is the manager of the Osaka Shosen Kaisha reports that the money and jewellery were left in a box, which is also missing. The theft occurred between 11 p.m. on Wednesday and 6 o'clock the next morning.

label: text
text: With the detection of the theft a chair coolie in the house was found to have disappeared. Suspicion rests on this man.

label: text
text: say you went to collect the money for this Bank?

label: text
text: Witness: No. I met him there. Mr. Jenkin: By arrangement? Witness: Yes.

label: text
text: Mr. Jenkin: Fok was a partner or shareholder in this venture of yours.

label: text
text: All Canton Money.

label: text
text: In answer to further questions, witness said that when he was minded to open a banking business, Fok had not in fact any shares. All the money in question was raised in Canton. None had been raised in Hongkong.

label: text
text: Mr. Jenkin: Whilst in Canton, did you and Fok meet Lum, the second defendant?

label: text
text:
Witness: No. I did not meet.
Lum until last year.

label: text
text: Mr. Jenkin: I put it to you that you and Fok did meet. Lum in Canton and that an arrangement was made that Lum should procure forged pages for the deposit. Look you were to get from the Wing On.

label: text
text: Witness: I deny that.

label: text
text: Mr. Jenkins: Will you then explain why there was this sudden activity in early April to collect this $51,000 which on your own showing was not used for months. Witness: It was not "sudden." I had organised the business and I had to collect money.

label: text
text: Mr. Jenkins: Did you intend to start the business at once on getting the money?

label: text
text: Witness: Yes, as soon as I could find premises.

label: text
text: Mr. Jenkin then cross-examined witness as to what arrangements he had made for starting the business when he got back from Canton with the money. Witness stated in reply that he had paid

label: text
text: bargain money to certain prospective fokis and had an office promised him over the Po Wa business in Queen's Road Central.

label: text
text: Mr. Jenkin: The account opened with the Industrial and Commercial Bank was solely for the funds of the Bank for which you collected money?

label: text
text: Mr. Jenkin: You are sure of that.

label: text
text: Witness: Yes.

label: text
text: Witness was then examined as to certain items in that account and he then admitted that $1,000 which was paid in was his own personal money.

label: text
text:
Mr. Jenkin: How is it, if you had a personal account in this bank as well as the account in the name of the Bank you say you were going to start, that you did not use the deposit book of your own personal account?
Witness replied that he thought it might be easier for this amount to go through the account of the Bank as it might be easier when it came to paying out.
Mr. Jenkin: I confess I cannot understand you. And with regard to an amount of $200 which on August 7 of that year you obtained from the alleged Bank account on a bearer cheque endorsed by you. What was that for?
Witness: It was for my brother to take up country for payment of family expenses.

label: text
text:
Mr. Jenkin: Do you mean to tell us as a man with considerable business and banking experience that the first thing you did with money you say was deposited for banking purposes by your partners was to take out an amount of family expenses?
Witness: That is so. The money was for family expenses. Mr. Zeitlyn concluded his examination of Au Kim-lui yesterday afternoon.

label: text
text: That he is believed to have acted under orders by the Canton Government in coming to Hongkong, in connection with the negotiations to end the present boycott, is stated by the local vernacular papers regarding the visit of Dr. Giri Tzafling.

label: text
text: Dr. Lam is described in the Chinese report as the Deputy Superintendent of Customs (Canton). Mr. Fu Ping-sheung is Superintendent of Customs and Commissioner for Foreign Affairs; and for a number of years the same official has held these two posts jointly. The conclusion is that Dr. Lam holds the position of Deputy Superintendent of Customs but he also is acting for Mr. Fu Ping-sheung in other matters.

label: text
text: Broadly translated, the report reads:—

label: text
text: "Dr. Lam arrived here from Canton on Tuesday. He conversed with the Hon. Mr. R. H. Then follows the reference to the peace negotiations.

label: text
text: The “China Mail” understands that three other gentlemen also came down with Dr. Lam. One of these was a Mr. Lam.

text: Although Dr. Lam has returned to Canton, the other three are still, as far as is known, in the Colony.

label: text
text: Over eighty passengers are alleged, in the "Kung Sheung Yat Fo," to have fallen into the hands of boycott pickets in Chinese territory near Macao, for whom ransoms were demanded.

label: text
text: After a running duel in waters near Chin Shan, a native boat was captured. Several kinds of weapons were used in the fight, it is stated, including machine-guns and cannon. The boat was ultimately boarded by pickets who took all the passengers to their depot. There, the report continues, they were made to communicate with their relatives, making that sums of money, varying from $80 to $120, should be paid to bring about their release.

label: paragraph_title
text: REFORMATORY FOR STREET

label: text
text: With a number of Clubs in the place, why not a Hongkong Street Urchins Club?

label: text
text: The idea has been furnished by the receipt of a report from the Ceylon Police who have instituted such a movement in Colombo with satisfactory results. "As an experiment a Club on similar lines has been started by the Hongkong Police and barely two weeks old; it promises to be a permanent one in making useful citizens of the waifs and strays in the Colony.

label: text
text: Well might the boys say "We are Seven", for that is the present membership of the Club. Details gathered show that their ages vary from 14 to 16 years, while residence in Hongkong since leaving the various Chinese districts from which they had all count from one to seven years. All but one lad who states he has a father in the country are without parents. During this period they have lived in the streets and carries on a miserable existence on the proceeds of pilfering and hawking.

label: text
text:
Clad in navy blue suits provided by the Poor Box funds in place of the rags in which they were found in the streets, the boys attract considerable attention while engaged in their new occupation of selling Chinese newspapers. With the confidence born of their new environment, they are happy and keen on their work.
At present the boys are provided with a room above the Central Magistracy. They are supplied with soap and towels and one of the stipulations is that they have a bath every day. Facilities are given to take part in games while otherwise free from their work of selling newspapers in the mornings and afternoons. Already a football has been supplied and the boys often engage in a little game on the compound. Arrangements have also been made with a school at Cochrane Street to teach them English and Chinese during their leisure hours at moderate fees to be borne by the boys themselves.
Although the wages earned at present make the boys self-supporting, it is hoped to find more remunerative employment for them later. They provide their own meals and pay 25 cents each a month as rent, this sum being placed to a fund for their benefit. Two have already started to save money, their savings bank books shewing sums of $1 and 40 cents.
Membership is secured on expressing a desire to join, but candidates must be physically fit and prove that they are bona fide waifors strays.
Sergeant Nolloth, in charge of the hawkers' department, presides over the Club and when more roomy quarters have been secured for the members they will be looked after by a responsible officer who would reside in the place.
The main idea is to eliminate petty crime among juveniles and this seems to be gradually achieved by the formation of the Club.

label: paragraph_title

label: text
text: Cruelty to a bullfinch was alleged against a Chinese youth by a European Sergeant who in his evidence at the Central Magistracy this morning stated that he saw the accused making the bird go round in circles to the delight of a crowd round him. The bird and a wing and a leg wrenched off. Fine $20.

label: text
text: A Shantung constable was charged at the Magistracy yesterday with misconduct. He was caught seated in an opium divan at Peal Street at a time when he should have been on duty in the street. His excuse that he went there to have a cup of tea did not satisfy the Magistrate, as Captain Bloxham produced a bad record. He was sent to prison for three months with hard labour.
